C004.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
C004.object: 10 years, but only if a major algorithmic breakthrough in continual learning occurs by 2027
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) 10 years, but only if a major algorithmic breakthrough in continual learning occurs by 2027]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic tracking of continual learning benchmarks (e.g., CORe50, CLEAR, Split-MNIST) and their performance trends vs. human-level transfer learning — If no major algorithmic breakthrough in continual learning is observed by 2027 (e.g., no system achieves >90% of human-level retention and forward transfer across diverse tasks), the hypothesis is refuted. Continued plateauing would indicate the 10-year AGI timeline is unlikely.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of AI research funding and publication trends in continual learning from 2025-2027, focusing on breakthrough indicators (e.g., new theoretical frameworks, orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains) — A major breakthrough would be visible through a sudden surge in high-impact papers, new funding initiatives, or paradigm shifts. Absence of such signals by 2027 would disconfirm the necessary condition for AGI within 10 years.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the computational and algorithmic lower bounds for continual learning (e.g., using complexity theory or information-theoretic models of catastrophic forgetting) — If formal proofs show that known algorithmic approaches cannot achieve human-level continual learning without a fundamentally new principle (e.g., synaptic consolidation mechanisms not yet discovered), then the hypothesis becomes less plausible, especially if no such principle emerges by 2027.

C005.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Survey of AI researchers' timelines for AGI (e.g., Müller & Bostock 2022 or similar repeated expert elicitation) — Provides direct probabilistic assessment of expert consensus on AGI timing, which can confirm or refute the 20-year claim if updated regularly.

[PATH:theoretical] Long-term trend analysis of compute and algorithmic efficiency (e.g., scaling laws from Kaplan et al. 2020, Hoffmann et al. 2022) — Extrapolates whether current rate of improvement in training compute, data, and model capabilities is sufficient to reach AGI within 20 years, based on known bottlenecks.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of historical AI capability milestones and their lead times (e.g., from narrow AI to transfer learning, including benchmarks like ARC-AGI) — Assesses whether past rate of progress in general intelligence benchmarks supports a 20-year timeline, using empirical evidence from the field.

C006.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Tracking progress on key AGI benchmarks (e.g., ARC-AGI, MMLU, HumanEval) and extrapolating scaling trends in compute and data efficiency — Empirical data on current AI capabilities and their rate of improvement can reveal whether progress is accelerating or plateauing, directly informing the likelihood of achieving AGI within 20 years.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of expert surveys on AGI timelines (e.g., AI Impacts, Müller & Bostock surveys) and their methodological critiques — Systematic review of expert opinions and the reasons behind their disagreements (e.g., assumptions about algorithmic breakthroughs vs. scaling) can highlight the robustness of the 20-year estimate and identify key uncertainties.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational and algorithmic requirements for AGI, such as the necessity of causal reasoning, common sense, and open-ended learning — If AGI requires fundamentally new architectures or learning paradigms not yet discovered, theoretical arguments about the difficulty of these challenges can support the hypothesis that 20 years is insufficient.

C007.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term forecasting surveys of AI researchers (e.g., Müller & Bostock 2018, annual AI Impacts surveys, or updated 2024-2025 expert elicitation studies) — Directly measures expert consensus on AGI timelines; a shift in median forecast from >20 years to <20 years would refute the hypothesis, while stability or lengthening would support it.

[PATH:empirical] Trend analysis of compute scaling and algorithmic efficiency (e.g., Epoch AI's tracking of training compute for large language models and reinforcement learning agents) — Empirical extrapolation of compute and data requirements to reach human-level performance across diverse tasks; if current trends suggest required resources exceed feasible growth within 20 years, the hypothesis is supported; if not, refuted.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal analysis of cognitive architectures and capability thresholds (e.g., Goertzel's patternist philosophy, or Bostrom's superintelligence pathway models) — Provides theoretical bounds on whether current AI paradigms (e.g., deep learning) can scale to general intelligence or require fundamental breakthroughs; identifies necessary but missing components (e.g., causal reasoning, common sense) that could delay or preclude AGI within 20 years.
